questions.question: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP?
questions.title: OLTP vs OLAP: Understanding the Two Database Workload Types
questions.direct_answer: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) handles high-frequency, short-lived transactions on current data -- like placing orders or updating account balances. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) handles complex analytical queries across large historical datasets -- like computing revenue trends or cohort analyses. They have opposing optimization requirements and are typically run on separate systems.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand why a single database rarely serves both workloads well and can explain the architectural pattern of separating transactional and analytical systems.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running analytics queries directly on the production OLTP database, which degrades transactional performance and risks locking issues.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the Lambda or Kappa architecture for feeding OLAP systems from OLTP sources, or mention modern HTAP databases like TiDB or AlloyDB that attempt to serve both.

sections.content: OLTP and OLAP represent two fundamentally different database workload profiles with opposing optimization strategies. OLTP systems are optimized for low-latency reads and writes on individual records. OLAP systems are optimized for high-throughput scans across millions of rows, often using columnar storage and vectorized execution. Running both on the same database causes contention and poor performance for each.
sections.title: Overview

sections.content:
| Dimension | OLTP | OLAP |
|---|---|---|
| Primary Purpose | Transactional operations (insert/update/delete) ✅ | Analytical queries (aggregations, trends) ✅ |
| Query Complexity | Simple, indexed lookups ✅ | Complex multi-table scans, GROUP BY ✅ |
| Data Volume per Query | Small (one or a few rows) ✅ | Large (millions of rows) ✅ |
| Concurrency | Thousands of short transactions ✅ | Few long-running queries ⚠️ |
| Storage Format | Row-oriented (good for row reads/writes) ✅ | Columnar (good for aggregations on few columns) ✅ |
| Normalization | Highly normalized (3NF) ✅ | Denormalized (star/snowflake schema) ⚠️ |
| Latency Target | Milliseconds ✅ | Seconds to minutes acceptable ⚠️ |
| Examples | PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle | Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse |
sections.title: Comparison Table

sections.content: Use OLTP for: user-facing features that create, read, or update individual records in real time -- orders, user accounts, inventory, payments. Use OLAP for: business intelligence dashboards, trend analysis, cohort reports, and data science workloads that aggregate data across millions of rows and long time ranges. In most architectures, OLTP data is replicated or streamed (via Debezium and Kafka) into a separate OLAP warehouse to avoid contention. HTAP databases like Google AlloyDB, TiDB, or CockroachDB attempt to serve both, but with trade-offs.
sections.title: When to Use Each
Building the OLTP-to-OLAP Data Pipeline
sections.content:
The bridge between OLTP and OLAP systems is a data pipeline that extracts changes from the transactional database and loads them into the analytical warehouse. The two dominant approaches are batch ETL and streaming CDC, and choosing between them depends on your freshness requirements.

Batch ETL runs on a schedule — hourly, nightly, or at a cadence matching your reporting needs. A job reads from the OLTP database (or its read replica to avoid production load), transforms the data into the warehouse's star schema, and loads it via bulk insert. Tools like Apache Airflow orchestrate these jobs with dependency tracking and retry logic. The advantage is simplicity and predictable resource usage. The disadvantage is latency: dashboards show data that is hours old, and debugging issues requires waiting for the next ETL run.

Streaming CDC uses Debezium to capture row-level changes from the OLTP database's transaction log (PostgreSQL WAL, MySQL binlog) and publish them to Kafka topics in real time. A downstream consumer — Kafka Connect with a BigQuery or Snowflake sink, or a custom Flink job — transforms and loads the changes into the warehouse continuously. Data freshness drops from hours to seconds. The trade-off is operational complexity: you are running Debezium, Kafka, and the sink connector as additional infrastructure with their own monitoring, alerting, and failure modes.

The star schema on the OLAP side denormalizes your normalized OLTP tables into fact tables (events, transactions) and dimension tables (customers, products, time). This structure optimizes for `GROUP BY` and `JOIN` performance in columnar engines. The transformation layer — whether batch or streaming — handles this denormalization, flattening normalized relations into wide rows.

For cost management in cloud warehouses, partition fact tables by date and set expiration policies on old partitions. A Snowflake table with 3 years of order data partitioned by month allows queries scoped to "last 90 days" to scan only 3 partitions instead of 36, dramatically reducing compute costs.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **OLTP: row-oriented, normalized, indexed for point lookups** — `WHERE id = ?` in milliseconds; schema designed to minimize write amplification on individual records
- **OLAP: columnar, denormalized, optimized for full scans and aggregates** — reading only the needed columns across millions of rows is orders of magnitude faster in columnar storage
- **Analytics on an OLTP database causes latency spikes** — a full table scan competes for I/O with concurrent transactions; always run reports on a read replica or dedicated warehouse
- **CDC + streaming is the standard separation pattern** — Debezium captures OLTP change events, Kafka transports them, the warehouse ingests continuously for near-real-time analytics
- **HTAP databases attempt both workloads** — TiDB and CockroachDB maintain row and columnar storage internally; useful when strict separation adds too much operational overhead

OLTP and OLAP are two database workload profiles that are almost impossible to optimize for simultaneously — which is why production systems separate them.

**OLTP — fast writes and reads on individual records**
- OLTP handles transactional operations: place an order, update inventory, create an account — each touches a few rows, runs in milliseconds, and happens thousands of times per second
- OLTP schemas are normalized to minimize write amplification — one fact in one place, so a single UPDATE keeps everything consistent; row-oriented storage makes reading and writing individual records fast

**OLAP — aggregates across millions of rows**
- OLAP is for analytical queries: total revenue by region this quarter, cohort retention over 90 days — these scan millions of rows, compute aggregates, and may run for minutes
- OLAP benefits from columnar storage — reading only the `revenue` column across 50 million rows is far faster in a columnar format (Parquet, BigQuery, Redshift) than reading full rows from a row-oriented OLTP table

**Why you can't run both on the same database**
- A long analytical query holds shared locks and competes for I/O with transactional queries — a full table scan during peak hours causes latency spikes across all concurrent OLTP operations on the same server
- The separation pattern: stream changes from the OLTP database via CDC (Debezium + Kafka) to a dedicated columnar warehouse; analytics run on the warehouse without affecting the transactional system

In interviews, describe the architecture: OLTP as the source of truth, a streaming layer, and a columnar warehouse for analytics. HTAP databases like TiDB attempt both workloads in one system by maintaining separate row and columnar storage internally — worth mentioning as a modern alternative.

questions.question: How do you design for high read throughput?
questions.title: Designing Databases for High Read Throughput
questions.direct_answer: Design for high read throughput by layering caching (application-level, distributed cache, HTTP cache), adding read replicas to distribute load, denormalizing hot query paths to avoid expensive joins, using materialized views or precomputed aggregates, and ensuring proper indexing. The goal is to reduce work per read and distribute reads across more hardware.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can reason systematically about read scaling and identify the right tool for each layer of the stack rather than jumping straight to database hardware upgrades.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Upgrading the database server as the first response to read performance issues, rather than introducing caching or read replicas which are cheaper and more effective.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the cache-aside pattern with TTL and cache invalidation strategy, and discuss how read replicas introduce replication lag that affects read-your-writes consistency.

sections.content: High read throughput requires reducing the work the database does per request, distributing reads across multiple machines, and serving repeated reads from faster caches. The strategy is a layered funnel: serve from memory first, fall through to replica, and hit the primary only for cache misses that need consistent data.
sections.title: Overview
Step 1: Add Caching Layers
sections.content: Implement cache-aside with Redis or Memcached for hot data. On read, check the cache first; on miss, read from DB and populate the cache with a TTL. Use local in-process caches (Caffeine) for data that is read thousands of times per second per instance. For HTTP APIs, set Cache-Control headers so upstream proxies and CDNs cache responses. Caching is the single most effective read throughput technique -- a Redis hit completes in under a millisecond and adds zero database load.

sections.title: Step 2: Add Read Replicas
sections.content: Configure read replicas using your database's streaming replication (PostgreSQL streaming replication, MySQL binlog replication). Route read-only queries -- reports, search, list views -- to replicas. Keep writes and reads requiring immediate consistency on the primary. In Spring, use @Transactional(readOnly = true) and configure a routing DataSource that sends read-only transactions to replicas. Be aware of replication lag: a replica may be milliseconds to seconds behind the primary, so avoid reading from a replica immediately after a write that the user must see.

sections.title: Step 3: Optimize Queries and Indexes
sections.content: Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to identify sequential scans and missing indexes. Add covering indexes to eliminate heap fetches. Denormalize frequently joined tables into a single wide table for query paths where join cost is significant. Create materialized views for expensive aggregations that are queried frequently but can tolerate slight staleness, and refresh them on a schedule or on write.

sections.title: Step 4: Denormalize Strategically
sections.content: Store precomputed or denormalized data for the hottest read paths. For example, maintain a cached_follower_count column on the users table rather than counting rows in the followers table on every profile view. Use event-driven updates (Kafka consumers or database triggers) to keep denormalized data fresh. Accept that this data may be slightly stale and design the UI to handle eventual consistency.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Cache-aside with TTL is the highest-leverage first step** — a Redis cache hit costs microseconds; a database query with a join costs milliseconds; at 10k req/s, that gap determines whether you need more infrastructure
- **Read replicas distribute SELECT load but introduce replication lag** — route reads to the primary for immediately-following writes to preserve read-your-writes consistency
- **Missing index before adding infrastructure** — a full table scan on 50M rows costs seconds; the right index turns it to milliseconds at zero hardware cost; profile first
- **Connection pooling prevents connection-creation bottleneck** — TCP handshake and auth per request is expensive at scale; HikariCP reuses connections across thousands of concurrent requests
- **Denormalization trades write cost for read speed** — pre-join hot paths and document what's duplicated, from where, and how it stays consistent when the source changes

High read throughput is a layered problem — the solution is identifying which layer can absorb the most load before a request reaches the database, then applying the right technique at each layer.

**Layer 1 — Cache before the database**
- The cheapest read is one that never touches the database — a response cached in Redis with a 60-second TTL serves thousands of requests from memory, which means the database sees one query per minute instead of thousands
- Cache-aside is the most common pattern: check Redis first, return if found, otherwise query the database, populate the cache, and return; the challenge is invalidation when the underlying data changes

**Layer 2 — Read replicas**
- Add PostgreSQL or MySQL read replicas to distribute SELECT queries — writes go to the primary, reads route to replicas via a load balancer or the application's data source configuration
- Replicas introduce replication lag — a user who just wrote a record may not see it on the first read from a replica; solve this with read-your-writes: route reads to the primary for a short window after a write

**Layer 3 — Query and schema optimization**
- Before adding hardware, check the execution plan — a missing index on a frequently filtered column can cause a full table scan on millions of rows; the right index eliminates the problem without any infrastructure change
- Denormalizing pre-joins frequently read tables trades storage and write complexity for read speed on hot paths

**Layer 4 — Connection pooling**
- Connection pooling (HikariCP, PgBouncer) prevents the overhead of creating a new database connection per request — at scale, connection establishment is a bottleneck before the database engine becomes one

Always profile before adding layers. A missing index often provides more improvement than adding a cache tier or a new replica.

questions.question: How do you handle soft deletes in database design?
questions.title: Soft Deletes in Database Design
questions.direct_answer: Soft deletes mark records as deleted without physically removing them from the database, typically with a deleted_at timestamp column or an is_deleted boolean. The record remains in the table and can be audited, restored, or referenced by foreign keys. The trade-offs are that every query must filter out deleted records and indexes become less efficient as the table accumulates ghost rows.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of the operational trade-offs of soft deletes and the ability to design a clean implementation that does not leak deleted data to users.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to add deleted_at filters to every query, allowing deleted records to appear in responses. Spring Boot's @SQLRestriction annotation on the entity is the standard mitigation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss partial indexes on deleted_at IS NULL to keep index size small, and the alternative of archiving old records to a separate table or audit log.

sections.content: Soft deletes preserve data for audit trails, compliance requirements, or undo functionality. Instead of DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = ?, the application sets deleted_at = now(). All other queries must then include WHERE deleted_at IS NULL to exclude these records.
sections.title: Overview
Code Example
Operational Patterns for Soft Delete Lifecycle Management
sections.content:
Soft deletes accumulate over time, and without a lifecycle management strategy, they degrade query performance, inflate storage costs, and create compliance risks. Three operational patterns address these concerns.

The first is scheduled hard-delete jobs. After a retention period (30 days, 90 days, or whatever your business requires for undo functionality), a background job permanently deletes soft-deleted records. This keeps tables lean and indexes efficient. Implement this as a partitioned batch job: delete in chunks of 1000 rows with a small sleep between batches to avoid lock contention and replication lag spikes. Use `DELETE FROM orders WHERE deleted_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '90 days' LIMIT 1000` in a loop rather than a single massive DELETE that locks the table.

The second is archive-then-purge. Before hard-deleting, copy soft-deleted records to an archive table or a cold storage system (S3 as Parquet files, or a separate PostgreSQL instance with cheaper storage). This preserves the data for legal or analytical purposes while removing it from the hot production tables. The archive table can have relaxed indexing and no partial-index constraints since it is only accessed for audits and legal holds.

The third pattern addresses GDPR and data privacy regulations. Soft delete alone does not satisfy the "right to be forgotten" — the personal data still exists in the database. For GDPR compliance, implement a separate anonymization step that replaces personally identifiable fields (name, email, address) with hashed or placeholder values while preserving the record structure for referential integrity. This is distinct from deletion: the record exists but contains no personal data. Track anonymization status with an `anonymized_at` timestamp column alongside `deleted_at`.

For foreign key relationships, soft-deleting a parent record that has active children creates orphan references. Decide on a policy: cascade the soft delete to children, prevent deletion if active children exist, or allow it and handle the "parent deleted" state in the UI. Document this policy per entity in your domain model documentation.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@SQLRestriction("deleted_at IS NULL")` prevents accidental leaks** — adds the filter to every JPA repository query automatically; without it, a custom query missing the clause exposes deleted records to end users
- **Standard indexes include soft-deleted rows** — records accumulate in the index even though they're never queried; a partial index on `deleted_at IS NULL` keeps the index aligned with actual query patterns
- **Partial unique index allows re-registration** — `UNIQUE WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` excludes deleted rows from the constraint, so a re-registered email doesn't conflict with a previously deleted account
- **Storage requires a purge policy** — soft deletes grow indefinitely; a background job must archive or hard-delete rows past the retention window to prevent unbounded table growth
- **`@SQLRestriction` (Hibernate 6+) replaces `@Where`** — use `@SQLRestriction` for Jakarta EE compatibility in modern Spring Boot applications

Soft deletes come up whenever an application needs audit history, undo functionality, or regulatory data retention. Instead of running DELETE, you set a `deleted_at` timestamp and treat the row as invisible to normal queries.

**How it works in practice**
- Add a `deleted_at TIMESTAMP NULL` column — rows with a non-null value are logically deleted, rows with null are active; every query that should exclude deleted records needs `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`
- In Spring Boot with JPA, `@SQLRestriction("deleted_at IS NULL")` on the entity class adds that filter automatically to every repository query — which means forgetting the clause in one custom query doesn't accidentally surface deleted data; but accessing deleted rows then requires a separate native query

**The index problem**
- A standard index on `user_id` includes all rows, deleted or not — as soft-deleted rows accumulate, the index grows and scans slow down even though those rows are never returned to users
- A partial index fixes this: `CREATE INDEX ON orders(user_id) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` — the index contains only active rows, so it stays small, precise, and fast for the queries that actually matter

**Trade-offs interviewers expect you to address**
- Storage grows without a purge policy — soft-deleted rows accumulate indefinitely; a background job should archive or hard-delete rows past the retention period
- Unique constraints break on re-registration — a unique index on `email` blocks re-use after soft-delete; a partial unique index `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` allows re-registration by excluding deleted rows from the constraint

questions.question: What is eventual consistency and how do you design for it?
questions.title: Eventual Consistency: What It Is and How to Design for It
questions.direct_answer: Eventual consistency is a consistency model where a distributed system guarantees that all replicas will converge to the same state eventually -- given no new updates -- but does not guarantee that any particular read will return the latest written value. Systems designed for eventual consistency must handle stale reads gracefully, use idempotent operations, and communicate uncertainty to users where appropriate.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the CAP theorem trade-off and can design application logic that works correctly with stale or out-of-order data.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming that eventual consistency means sometimes wrong -- it means temporarily inconsistent, not incorrect. Well-designed eventually consistent systems produce correct results once the system settles.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss conflict resolution strategies (last-writer-wins, vector clocks, CRDTs), the read-your-writes consistency pattern, and how to use version fields or timestamps to detect staleness.

sections.content: The CAP theorem states that a distributed system can guarantee at most two of: Consistency (every read returns the latest write), Availability (every request receives a response), and Partition Tolerance (the system works despite network partitions). Since partition tolerance is a network reality, systems choose between CP (consistent but may be unavailable during partition) and AP (available but may return stale data). AP systems use eventual consistency.
sections.title: Overview
Code Example
Implementing Read-Your-Writes and Conflict Resolution Patterns
sections.content:
Eventual consistency is a system-level property, but users experience it at the individual request level. The read-your-writes pattern is the most important UX technique for making eventual consistency invisible to users in the common case.

The simplest implementation routes the user's reads to the primary database for a short window after they perform a write. In Spring Boot, this means setting a cookie or session attribute with a timestamp after any write operation, and having a filter check this timestamp on subsequent reads. If the write occurred within the last 5 seconds, route the read to the primary via `AbstractRoutingDataSource`; otherwise, route to a replica. This is not globally consistent — other users may still see stale data — but it ensures the writing user sees their own change immediately.

A more sophisticated approach returns the written entity directly in the write response and uses client-side state management (React state, Redux store) to optimistically display the change without making a follow-up read. The UI shows the locally updated state while the backend propagates the change to replicas in the background. This eliminates the need for any special read routing at the cost of client-side complexity.

For conflict resolution in multi-writer scenarios, the choice depends on your domain's tolerance for data loss. Last-writer-wins with `@Version` optimistic locking is the simplest: the second writer receives an `OptimisticLockException` and must retry with the latest version. This is correct for most business applications where concurrent edits to the same record are rare.

For collaborative editing scenarios — shared documents, wikis, or configuration that multiple operators modify — consider Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs). A grow-only set or a last-writer-wins register with Lamport timestamps allows concurrent updates to merge automatically without coordination. Libraries like Automerge implement CRDTs for JSON documents. The trade-off is that CRDTs constrain your data model — not every operation can be made commutative — but for the operations they support, they eliminate conflict resolution entirely.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Eventual ≠ incorrect — it means temporarily divergent** — replicas converge after propagation; a stale read is a timing window, not corrupt data
- **Read-your-writes requires routing to the same source** — after a write, route the user's immediate reads to the primary or write replica to guarantee they see their own changes before propagation completes
- **Idempotent operations are required for safe retries** — `SET balance = 100` applied twice is safe; `balance - 10` applied twice loses money; design all operations to produce the same result on repeat execution
- **Last-writer-wins silently discards concurrent updates** — if two writes race on the same key, one is lost; use version vectors or CRDTs for data that must survive concurrent modification without data loss
- **Monotonic read consistency prevents time travel** — once a session reads a value, subsequent reads in that session must not return an older value; bind reads within a session to the same replica

Eventual consistency is one of those terms that sounds alarming until you understand what it actually means. It doesn't mean the system gives wrong answers — it means replicas may be briefly out of sync but will converge to the same state given enough time and no further writes.

**What it means in a distributed system**
- When a write lands on one node, it propagates to other nodes asynchronously — which means a read on a different replica immediately after the write may return the old value, not because the data is wrong, but because the update is still in transit
- Given enough time with no new writes, all replicas converge to the same value — "eventually" is about the propagation window, not about correctness

**The CAP theorem context**
- CAP says a distributed system under network partition must choose between consistency (every read returns the latest write) and availability (every request gets a response) — eventual consistency is the choice to prioritize availability
- Cassandra, DynamoDB, and CouchDB are AP systems: they stay available during partitions and converge afterward; traditional RDBMS with synchronous replication is CP: it may reject writes during partition to maintain consistency

**Designing applications for eventual consistency**
- Read-your-writes consistency: route a user's reads to the primary or the same replica they wrote to for a short window after a write — so the user always sees their own changes even if other replicas haven't caught up
- Idempotent operations handle duplicate delivery: if an event is re-processed due to a retry, the result must be identical to processing it once — `SET balance = 100` is safe; `balance - 10` run twice is not
- Last-writer-wins by timestamp is the simplest conflict resolution strategy but loses data when two writes race; CRDTs handle specific data types without data loss under concurrent writes

Eventual consistency is a deliberate trade-off, not a failure mode — the system is correct, just temporarily partitioned in time.

seo.metaTitle: Eventual Consistency Explained -- Design Patterns in Java | Interview Prep
seo.metaDescription: Understand eventual consistency, the CAP theorem, and how to design Java systems for stale reads, idempotency, and conflict resolution in distributed databases.

speakable_v2.hook: Eventual consistency is one of those terms that sounds alarming until you understand what it actually means.

beats.text: The CAP theorem states that a distributed system can guarantee at most two of: Consistency (every read returns the latest write), Availability (every request receives a response), and Partition Tolerance (the system works despite network partitions). Since partition tolerance is a network reality, systems choose between CP (consistent but may be unavailable during partition) and AP (available but may return stale data). AP systems use eventual consistency.

steps: Eventual consistency is a system-level property, but users experience it at the individual request level.
The read-your-writes pattern is the most important UX technique for making eventual consistency invisible to users in the common case.
The simplest implementation routes the user's reads to the primary database for a short window after they perform a write.
In Spring Boot, this means setting a cookie or session attribute with a timestamp after any write operation, and having a filter check this timestamp on subsequent reads.
If the write occurred within the last 5 seconds, route the read to the primary via AbstractRoutingDataSource; otherwise, route to a replica.
This is not globally consistent — other users may still see stale data — but it ensures the writing user sees their own change immediately.

items: Eventual ≠ incorrect — it means temporarily divergent — replicas converge after propagation; a stale read is a timing window, not corrupt data Read-your-writes requires routing to the same source — after a write, route the user's immediate reads to the primary or write replica to guarantee they see their own changes before propagation completes Idempotent operations are required for safe retries — SET balance = 100 applied twice is safe; balance - 10 applied twice loses money; design all operations to produce the same result on repeat execution Last-writer-wins silently discards concurrent updates — if two writes race on the same key, one is lost; use version vectors or CRDTs for data that must survive concurrent modification without data loss Monotonic read consistency prevents time travel — once a session reads a value, subsequent reads in that session must not return an older value; bind reads within a session to the same replica

beats.text: Assuming that eventual consistency means sometimes wrong -- it means temporarily inconsistent, not incorrect. Well-designed eventually consistent systems produce correct results once the system settles.

speakable_v2.cap: What it means in a distributed system When a write lands on one node, it propagates to other nodes asynchronously — which means a read on a different replica immediately after the write may return.

questions.question: What are the key differences between InnoDB and MyISAM storage engines in MySQL?
questions.title: InnoDB vs MyISAM Storage Engines
questions.direct_answer: InnoDB is the default MySQL engine offering ACID transactions, foreign keys, row-level locking, and crash recovery. MyISAM is an older engine with faster read performance for non-transactional workloads but lacks transactions, foreign key support, and uses table-level locking. For most modern Java/Spring Boot applications, InnoDB is the correct choice.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests understanding of MySQL internals, when to choose the right storage engine, and awareness of transactional guarantees critical for production Java applications.

sections.title: InnoDB vs MyISAM — Why It Matters
sections.content: MySQL supports multiple storage engines that handle how data is physically stored and retrieved. The two most historically significant are InnoDB (default since MySQL 5.5) and MyISAM (legacy default). Choosing the wrong engine can lead to data corruption, poor concurrency, or missing constraint enforcement in your Spring Boot application.

sections.title: InnoDB vs MyISAM Feature Comparison
sections.caption: InnoDB vs MyISAM Feature Comparison
sections.content:
### InnoDB vs MyISAM Feature Comparison

| Feature | InnoDB | MyISAM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ACID Transactions | ✅ Full support | ❌ Not supported |
| Foreign Keys | ✅ Enforced | ❌ Ignored |
| Locking Granularity | ✅ Row-level | ⚠️ Table-level |
| Crash Recovery | ✅ Automatic via redo log | ❌ Manual repair needed |
| Full-Text Search | ✅ Since MySQL 5.6 | ✅ Native support |
| Read Performance (no concurrency) | ⚠️ Slightly slower | ✅ Faster |
| Write Concurrency | ✅ High (row locks) | ❌ Low (table locks) |
| MVCC | ✅ Supported | ❌ Not supported |
| Spring/JPA Compatibility | ✅ Full | ⚠️ Partial (no rollback) |
| Compressed Tables | ✅ Supported | ⚠️ Limited |

sections.title: Production notes
sections.content:
### Operational checklist for Spring Boot + InnoDB

When you scaffold entities with JPA, confirm migrations explicitly set `ENGINE=InnoDB` (some older templates still omitted it). In production, pair transactional services with InnoDB so retry policies and outbox patterns actually mean something: a rolled-back service method should leave no persisted rows, which MyISAM cannot guarantee. If you inherit MyISAM tables, plan a low-risk migration window: `ALTER TABLE ... ENGINE=InnoDB` copies the table—test duration on a clone first, watch disk space, and temporarily cap application concurrency while the DDL runs. Finally, teach junior developers that “storage engine” is not cosmetic: it changes locking, backups, and replication behavior under failure.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **InnoDB: row-level locking vs MyISAM table-level locking** — a MyISAM UPDATE blocks every concurrent write on the entire table; an InnoDB UPDATE blocks only rows with conflicting keys
- **InnoDB: ACID transactions; MyISAM: none** — MyISAM has no rollback; a crashed multi-statement operation leaves data in a partially written state with no recovery path
- **InnoDB enforces foreign keys; MyISAM parses but ignores them** — declaring a FK on a MyISAM table compiles without error but never enforces referential integrity at runtime
- **InnoDB full-text search since MySQL 5.6** — the last practical reason to use MyISAM is gone; FULLTEXT indexes work on InnoDB tables in all modern MySQL versions
- **ALTER TABLE t ENGINE=InnoDB migrates MyISAM tables** — rebuilds the table with full InnoDB capabilities; required before enabling FK constraints or transactions on legacy tables

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
InnoDB and MyISAM are the two MySQL storage engines that come up most in interviews — InnoDB has been the default since MySQL 5.5 and the right choice for virtually every modern application.

**InnoDB — the default for good reason**
- InnoDB supports full ACID transactions, which means a multi-statement operation like debit account A and credit account B either both succeed or both roll back on crash — something MyISAM simply cannot do
- Row-level locking means concurrent writers block each other only when they touch the same row; MyISAM uses table-level locking, which means a single UPDATE blocks every other write on the table
- InnoDB enforces foreign key constraints at the database level, which means referential integrity is guaranteed even if the application has a bug; MyISAM ignores foreign key declarations entirely

**MyISAM — where it still exists**
- MyISAM was the historical default before MySQL 5.5 and is still present in legacy codebases; its main advantage was slightly faster reads on simple SELECT-heavy workloads with no concurrent writes
- Full-text search in older MySQL versions required MyISAM — but InnoDB has supported full-text indexes since MySQL 5.6, removing the last real reason to use MyISAM in new development
- If you encounter a MyISAM table in an existing system, the migration path to InnoDB is `ALTER TABLE t ENGINE=InnoDB` — it rebuilds the table with full InnoDB capabilities

For any new table in a Spring Boot application: InnoDB. The transaction and row-locking guarantees are non-negotiable for any data that matters, and full-text search, spatial queries, and all other specialized capabilities are available in InnoDB today.
